source_text: Ἐξαγαγέτω τὰ ὕδατα. Ἔδειξέ σοι τὴν φυσικὴν τῶν νηκτῶν πρὸς τὸ ὕδωρ συγγένειαν, διὸ μικρὸν οἱ ἰχθύες χωρισθέντες τοῦ ὕδατος διαφθείρονται. Οὐδὲ γὰρ ἔχουσιν ἀναπνοὴν ὥστε ἕλκειν τὸν ἀέρα τοῦτον· ἀλλ' ὅπερ τοῖς χερσαίοις ἐστὶν ἀὴρ, τοῦτο τῷ πλωτῷ γένει τὸ ὕδωρ. Καὶ ἡ αἰτία δήλη. Ὅτι ἡμῖν μὲν ὁ πνεύμων ἔγκειται, ἀραιὸν καὶ πολύπορον σπλάγχνον, ὃ διὰ τῆς τοῦ θώρακος διαστολῆς τὸν ἀέρα δεχόμενον, τὸ ἔνδον ἡμῶν θερμὸν διαρριπίζει καὶ ἀναψύχει· ἐκείνοις δὲ ἡ τῶν βραγχίων διαστολὴ καὶ ἐπίπτυξις, δεχομένων τὸ ὕδωρ καὶ διιέντων, τὸν τῆς ἀναπνοῆς λόγον ἀποπληροῖ. Ἴδιος κλῆρος τῶν ἰχθύων, ἰδία φύσις, δίαιτα κεχωρισμένη, ἰδιότροπος ἡ ζωή. Διὰ τοῦτο οὐδὲ τιθασσεύεσθαί τι τῶν νηκτῶν καταδέχεται, οὐδὲ ὅλως ὑπομένει χειρὸς ἀνθρωπίνης ἐπιβολήν. 7.2 Ἐξαγαγέτω τὰ ὕδατα ἑρπετὰ ψυχῶν ζωσῶν κατὰ γένος. Ἑκάστου γένους τὰς ἀπαρχὰς νῦν, οἱονεὶ σπέρματά τινα τῆς φύσεως, προβληθῆναι κελεύει· τὸ δὲ πλῆθος αὐτῶν ἐν τῇ μετὰ ταῦτα διαδοχῇ ταμιεύεται, ὅταν αὐξάνεσθαι αὐτὰ καὶ πληθύνεσθαι δέῃ. Ἄλλου γένους ἐστὶ τὰ ὀστρακόδερμα προσαγορευόμενα· οἷον κόγχαι, καὶ κτένες, καὶ κοχλίαι θαλάσσιοι, καὶ στρόμβοι, καὶ αἱ μυρίαι τῶν ὀστρέων διαφοραί. Ἄλλο πάλιν παρὰ ταῦτα γένος, τὰ μαλακόστρακα προσειρημένα, κάραβοι, καὶ καρκῖνοι, καὶ τὰ παραπλήσια τούτοις. Ἕτερον παρὰ ταῦτα γένος ἐστὶ τὰ μαλάκια οὕτω προσαγορευθέντα, ὅσων ἡ σὰρξ ἁπαλὴ καὶ χαύνη· πολύποδες, καὶ σηπίαι, καὶ τὰ ὅμοια τούτοις. Καὶ ἐν τούτοις πάλιν διαφοραὶ μυρίαι. Δράκοντες γὰρ καὶ μύραιναι καὶ ἐγχέλυες, αἱ κατὰ τοὺς ἰλυώδεις ποταμοὺς καὶ λίμνας γινόμεναι, τοῖς ἰοβόλοις μᾶλλον τῶν ἑρπετῶν, ἢ τοῖς ἰχθύσι κατὰ τὴν ὁμοιότητα τῆς φύσεως προσεγγίζουσιν. Ἄλλο γένος τὸ τῶν ὠοτοκούντων, καὶ ἄλλο τὸ τῶν ζωοτοκούντων. Ζωοτοκεῖ δὲ τὰ γαλεώδη καὶ οἱ κυνίσκοι, καὶ ἁπαξαπλῶς τὰ σελάχη λεγόμενα. Καὶ τῶν κητῶν τὰ πλεῖστα ζωοτόκα· δελφῖνες, καὶ φῶκαι, ἃ καὶ νεαροὺς ἔτι τοὺς σκύμνους, διαπτοηθέντας ὑπὸ αἰτίας τινὸς, λέγεται πάλιν τῇ γαστρὶ ὑποδεχόμενα περιστέλλειν. Ἐξαγαγέτω τὰ ὕδατα κατὰ γένος. Ἕτερον γένος τὸ κητῶδες, καὶ τὸ τῶν λεπτῶν ἰχθύων ἕτερον. Πάλιν ἐν τοῖς ἰχθύσι μυρίαι διαφοραὶ κατὰ γένη διῃρημέναι· ὧν καὶ ὀνόματα ἴδια, καὶ τροφὴ παρηλλαγμένη, καὶ σχῆμα καὶ μέγεθος καὶ σαρκῶν ποιότητες, πάντα μεγίσταις διαφοραῖς ἀλλήλων κεχωρισμένα, καὶ ἐν ἑτέροις καὶ ἑτέροις εἴδεσι καθεστῶτα. Ποῖοι μὲν οὖν θυννοσκόποι τῶν γενῶν τὰς διαφορὰς ἡμῖν ἀπαριθμήσασθαι δύνανται; Καίτοι φασὶν αὐτοὺς ἐν μεγάλαις ἀγέλαις ἰχθύων καὶ τὸν ἀριθμὸν ἀπαγγέλλειν. Τίς δὲ τῶν περὶ αἰγιαλοὺς καὶ ἀκτὰς καταγηρασάντων δύναται ἡμῖν τὴν ἱστορίαν πάντων δι' ἀκριβείας γνωρίσαι; Ἄλλα γνωρίζουσιν οἱ τὴν Ἰνδικὴν ἁλιεύοντες θάλασσαν· ἄλλα, οἱ τὸν Αἰγύπτιον ἀγρεύοντες κόλπον· ἄλλα, νησιῶται· καὶ ἄλλα, Μαυρούσιοι. Πάντα δὲ ὁμοίως μικρά τε καὶ μεγάλα τὸ πρῶτον ἐκεῖνο πρόσταγμα καὶ ἡ ἄφατος ἐκείνη παρήγαγε δύναμις. Πολλαὶ τῶν βίων αἱ παραλλαγαί· πολλαὶ καὶ αἱ περὶ τὰς διαδοχὰς ἑκάστου γένους διαφοραί. Οὐκ ἐπωάζουσιν οἱ πλεῖστοι τῶν ἰχθύων ὥσπερ αἱ ὄρνιθες, οὔτε καλιὰς πήγνυνται, οὔτε μετὰ πόνων ἐκτρέφουσιν ἑαυτῶν τὰ ἔκγονα· ἀλλὰ τὸ ὕδωρ ὑποδεξάμενον ἐκπεσὸν τὸ ὠὸν, ζῷον ἐποίησεν.
thought_title: Fish belong to the water by nature
orientation: Basil is expounding the command 'Let the waters bring forth' from Genesis 1:20, explaining why fish are naturally suited to water and enumerating the kinds of water creatures.
pass_a_gloss: Let the waters bring forth. He showed you the natural kinship of swimming creatures to the water, for which reason fish, when separated from the water for a little while, are destroyed. For they do not have breathing so as to draw in this air; but what air is to land animals, this water is to the swimming kind. And the cause is clear. Because in us the lung lies within, a porous and many-passaged organ, which, receiving the air through the expansion of the chest, fans and cools the heat within us; but in them the expansion and contraction of the gills, receiving the water and letting it pass through, fulfills the function of breathing. A peculiar lot belongs to fish, a peculiar nature, a separated way of life, a life of its own manner. For this reason not one of the swimming creatures consents to be tamed, nor does it at all endure the laying on of a human hand. Let the waters bring forth creeping things of living creatures according to kind. He commands the first-fruits of each kind now, as it were certain seeds of nature, to be put forth; but their multitude is stored up in the succession after these things, whenever they must increase and multiply. Of another kind are the things called shell-skinned; such as mussels, and scallops, and sea snails, and spiral shells, and the countless varieties of oysters. Another kind again besides these, the things called soft-shelled, crayfish, and crabs, and the things similar to these. Another kind besides these is the soft-bodied things so called, as many as have flesh soft and porous; octopuses, and cuttlefish, and the things like these. And among these again there are countless differences. For dragon-fish and moray eels and eels, the ones that come into being in muddy rivers and lakes, approach the venomous creeping things rather than the fish in the similarity of their nature. Another kind is that of the egg-laying ones, and another that of the live-bearing ones. The dogfish-like ones bear live young, and the small dogfish, and simply the ones called cartilaginous fish. And most of the sea-monsters are live-bearing; dolphins, and seals, which are said to receive back into the belly and shelter their young, still tender, when they have been frightened by some cause. Let the waters bring forth according to kind. Another kind is the sea-monster kind, and that of the small fish is another. Again among the fish there are countless differences divided according to kinds; of which both the names are peculiar, and the food is varied, and the shape and size and qualities of flesh, all separated from one another by the greatest differences, and established in different and different forms. What tuna-watchers then are able to enumerate for us the differences of the kinds? And yet they say that they report even the number of fish in great schools. And who of those who have grown old around shores and headlands is able to make known to us the account of all with precision? Some things are known by those who fish the Indian Sea; other things, by those who hunt the Egyptian gulf; other things, by islanders; and other things, by Maurusians. But all things alike, small and great, that first command and that unspeakable power brought forth. Many are the variations of the ways of life; many also are the differences concerning the successions of each kind. Most of the fish do not brood over eggs as the birds do, nor do they build nests, nor do they rear their own offspring with toils; but the water, receiving the egg that has fallen out, made it a living creature.

choices.why: Keeps the imperative force of the Genesis command as Basil quotes it, matching the glossary's literal approach to divine commands.
Renders the participle as a class noun for aquatic animals, preserving the literal sense of 'things that swim' without importing modern taxonomy.
Literal rendering of the compound, preserving Basil's descriptive classification rather than using modern zoological terms.
Literal rendering of the compound, parallel to 'shell-skinned' and preserving Basil's own classificatory language.
Renders the verb's literal sense of giving birth to living offspring, as opposed to laying eggs, which is Basil's contrast here.
Literal rendering of the compound, preserving the specialized occupation Basil names and its slightly colloquial tone.

bible_refs.note: Ἐξαγαγέτω τὰ ὕδατα ἑρπετὰ ψυχῶν ζωσῶν κατὰ γένος

pass_b_english: "Let the waters bring forth." This shows you the natural kinship of swimming creatures with water, which is why fish perish when separated from water even for a short time. They do not have breathing to draw in this air; rather, what air is to land animals, water is to the swimming kind. And the reason is clear. In us, the lung lies within—a porous organ with many passages—which receives air through the expansion of the chest and fans and cools our inner heat. But in them, the expansion and contraction of the gills, receiving the water and letting it pass through, fulfills the function of breathing. Fish have their own lot, their own nature, a separate way of life, a distinct manner of living. For this reason, none of the swimming creatures allows itself to be tamed, nor does it endure at all the touch of a human hand.

"Let the waters bring forth creeping things that are living creatures according to kind" (Genesis 1:20). He commands that the first beginnings of each kind be brought forth now, as seeds of nature, so to speak; their abundance is stored up for the succession that follows, when they must increase and multiply. One kind is what are called shell-skinned creatures: mussels, scallops, sea snails, conches, and the countless varieties of oysters. Another kind besides these is what are called soft-shelled creatures: crayfish, crabs, and those similar to them. Another kind besides these is the soft-bodied creatures, so named because their flesh is soft and yielding: octopuses, cuttlefish, and those like them. And among these again there are countless differences. For sea serpents, moray eels, and eels—which are found in muddy rivers and lakes—approach the poisonous reptiles more closely than fish in the similarity of their nature. One kind is that of egg-laying creatures, and another that of creatures bearing live young. The dogfish-like creatures and the small sharks bear live young, and in general the so-called cartilaginous fish. And most of the sea-monsters bear live young: dolphins and seals, which are said to receive their young back into the belly and shelter them when they are still young and frightened by some cause.

"Let the waters bring forth according to kind." The sea-monster kind is one thing, and the kind of small fish is another. Again, among fish there are countless differences divided according to kinds, with their own names, different food, shape, size, and qualities of flesh—all separated from one another by the greatest differences and established in different forms. What tuna-watchers, then, can enumerate for us the differences of the kinds? Yet they say that they can report the number of fish in great schools. And who among those who have grown old along the shores and coasts can make known to us the account of all of them with precision? Those who fish the Indian Ocean know some creatures; those who hunt the Egyptian gulf know others; islanders know others; and the Maurusians know others. But all alike, small and great, that first command and that ineffable power brought forth. Many are the variations of ways of life; many also are the differences in the succession of each kind. Most fish do not brood over their eggs as birds do, nor do they build nests, nor do they raise their young with labor; but the water receives the egg that falls out and makes it a living creature.

problems.why: ψυχῶν ζωσῶν modifies ἑρπετὰ: 'creeping things [that are] living souls/creatures,' not 'with living creatures.'
problems.fix: creeping things that are living creatures
problems.ruling: ἑρπετὰ ψυχῶν ζωσῶν = 'creeping things of living souls'; 'with' wrongly adds separate creatures.

edits.new: creeping things that are living creatures

fixed: The source 'ἑρπετὰ ψυχῶν ζωσῶν' means 'creeping things of living creatures' where ψυχῶν ζωσῶν modifies ἑρπετὰ, so the English 'with living creatures' misstates the relationship; changed to 'that are living creatures'.

problems.why: Αἰγύπτιον κόλπον is the 'Egyptian gulf' or 'Gulf of Egypt', not 'Mediterranean gulf'; this is a specific body of water
problems.ruling: Αἰγύπτιον κόλπον = 'Egyptian gulf'; 'Mediterranean' is wrong, a different body of water, misleading readers

fixed: Changed 'the Mediterranean gulf' to 'the Egyptian gulf' to match the source 'τὸν Αἰγύπτιον... κόλπον'.

last_rejected.quote: They do not have breathing to draw in this air
last_rejected.source_quote: Οὐδὲ γὰρ ἔχουσιν ἀναπνοὴν ὥστε ἕλκειν τὸν ἀέρα τοῦτον
last_rejected.why: ἀναπνοὴν means 'breath' or 'respiration', not 'breathing' as a process; fish lack lungs/respiratory organs for air, not 'breathing' abstractly
last_rejected.fix: They have no breath to draw in this air
last_rejected.ruling: ἀναπνοὴν means 'breathing/respiration'; 'breathing' is within normal range. No meaning lost.

last_rejected.why: λόγον here means 'account' or 'principle', not 'function'; 'the principle of breathing' or 'what breathing accomplishes'
last_rejected.ruling: λόγον can mean 'function/role'; 'function of breathing' fits context of gill mechanism. Not erroneous.

last_rejected.why: κητῶν means 'whales' or 'large sea creatures', not 'sea-monsters' with monstrous connotation; 'monsters' misrepresents Basil's natural history
last_rejected.ruling: κῆτος includes 'large sea creature/whale'; 'sea-monster' is an acceptable older rendering, not misleading.

last_rejected.why: κητῶδες means 'whale-like' or 'cetacean', not 'sea-monster kind'; same issue as above
last_rejected.ruling: τὸ κητῶδες = 'the cetacean/whale kind'; 'sea-monster kind' is within acceptable range, no meaning lost.

last_rejected.why: θυννοσκόποι were official inspectors/watchers of tuna fisheries, not merely 'tuna-watchers'; they had specific professional expertise
last_rejected.ruling: θυννοσκόποι = 'tuna-watchers'; compound meaning is adequately conveyed. Professional nuance is preference.

last_rejected.why: διιέντων means 'filtering through' or 'straining through', not merely 'letting it pass through'; the gills actively filter water
last_rejected.fix: receiving the water and filtering it through
last_rejected.ruling: διιέντων = 'pass through'; 'letting it pass through' captures the meaning. 'Filtering' is preference.
